I like the skip but my inner historybuff/pedant was brought out by this:

◾A rock opera chronicling the rise and fall of the Roman emperor Octavian

First, that would be the Emperor Augustus, he dropped the Octavian (technically Octavius but Octavian is an accepted version) long before he rose to power.
Second, what fall? Augustus never lost power and died as the ruler of Rome.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I like it. Two nits to pick though:

1. 960 depicts "three of the nine Muses", but lists a heretofore unknown Muse in addition to the nine commonly known. I suggest removing the "nine".
2. I think this should be Safe instead of Euclid. If you can take an object and put it in a room, and it doesn't do anything unless it's messed with, then it's Safe.

And I wouldn't worry too much about people adding crap to your article's research log— you can always take out any changes you don't like.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Thank you! I'm still new at this, so I suppose I need some pointers on setting research boundaries, but I'm happy to amend whatever needs amending.
I do realize it's fairly close to being a cliche, but I was hoping it was original enough to avoid it. I hadn't thought of what the scientific advances might eventually do, though- that's a possibility I'm not particularly comfortable with, now that I'm thinking about it.
It feels odd having to justify it, though. I've always felt like if you need to justify something, you didn't do a good enough job when you were making it… Still, I'll do what I can.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Dr. ███████ is standing in his workshop, screaming about the need for ██, ████, and ███████!

Dr. ███████ has begun a mysterious construction!

Sorry, couldn't resist.

Interesting idea, but if people request to write future 'results' from letting people touch it, we have to be careful with what they're allowed to do. This seems *close* to an "SCP what can make other SCP's". Not quite, as the result is often scientific research (in the final stage), but future people may accidentally overstep that line.

Still, nicely written! I quite like it.
